draft.title: Cognitive development
card: Cognitive development is the growth of thinking, memory, problem solving and reasoning across life. It builds step by step, and each stage uses what came before.
Infants first learn through senses and movement. Around the end of the first year, many learn object permanence: an object still exists when it is out of sight.
Children's thinking grows more logical. They use language and imagination, and they can later work through problems with real objects and events.
In adolescence, many people can reason about abstract ideas, such as fairness or freedom, and can plan ahead and think about possible outcomes.
draft.remember: Thinking grows from sensing and acting to reasoning about ideas.

a.q: Which example shows a child has developed object permanence?
opts: A baby looks for a toy that was hidden under a cloth
A baby smiles when a carer enters the room
A baby cries when a stranger picks them up
A baby copies the sound of a word
a.why: Searching for a hidden toy shows the baby knows it still exists out of sight. Smiling at a carer and crying at a stranger show emotional and social responses. Copying a sound shows learning, but not that objects exist unseen.
a.clue: Which baby acts as if something is still there when it cannot be seen?

b.q: Which situation best shows abstract reasoning?
opts: Ravi, 15, debates whether a law can be fair to everyone
Ravi, 15, remembers the way to his school
Ravi, 15, builds a model from a set of instructions
Ravi, 15, learns a new song by hearing it often
b.why: Debating whether a law can be fair means thinking about an idea, not a thing he can see or touch. Remembering a route, following instructions and learning a song all involve thinking, but each works with concrete things or events.
b.clue: Look for thinking about an idea, not a thing you can touch.

a.best: A baby looks for a toy that was hidden under a cloth

b.best: Ravi, 15, debates whether a law can be fair to everyone

card: Cognitive development is the growth of thinking, memory, problem solving and reasoning across life. It builds step by step, and each stage uses what came before.
Infants first learn through senses and movement. Around the end of the first year, many learn object permanence: an object still exists when it is out of sight.

In adolescence, many people can reason about abstract ideas, such as fairness or freedom, and can plan ahead and think about possible outcomes.
proposal.remember: Thinking grows from sensing and acting to reasoning about ideas.

a.q: Which example shows a child has developed object permanence?
opts: A baby lifts a cloth to find a toy she saw hidden there
A baby smiles each time her carer walks into the room
A baby cries when a stranger lifts her out of her cot
A baby copies the sound of a word her carer just said
a.why: Lifting the cloth shows the baby knows the toy still exists when she cannot see it. Smiling at a carer happens while the carer is in sight, so it shows a social response, not object permanence. Crying and copying a sound do not show she knows unseen objects still exist.
a.clue: Which baby acts as if something is still there when it cannot be seen?

b.q: Which situation best shows abstract reasoning?
opts: Ravi, 15, argues about whether it is ever right to lie
Ravi, 15, remembers which bus to catch to his school
Ravi, 15, assembles a bookshelf using the printed steps
Ravi, 15, learns a new song by hearing it many times
b.why: Whether lying is ever right is a question about an idea, not a thing he can see or touch. Following the bookshelf steps uses logical thinking, but it works with real objects. Remembering a bus and learning a song use memory of concrete things.
b.clue: Look for thinking about an idea, not a thing you can touch.
